entry.title: Generalized survival energy models with exogenous covariates for mortality prediction

link.title: Generalized survival energy models with exogenous covariates for mortality prediction

entry.content:
We develop a generalized survival energy model that relates mortality to social and economic conditions through a latent energy process. Death occurs when this process first reaches or crosses zero. Environmental covariates enter the coefficients governing depletion, recovery, fluctuations and accumulated damage, yielding lifetime distributions conditional on the environmental path. We derive these distributions for diffusion and inverse Gaussian specifications and describe their numerical evaluation. An application to Japanese male and female mortality data assesses predictive performance against Cairns–Blake–Dowd benchmarks. Conditional on realized environmental paths, the selected inverse Gaussian models achieve small prediction errors comparable to those of the benchmarks. The framework also provides a model-based interpretation of how environmental changes affect mortality through the rate of damage accumulation or the magnitude of energy fluctuations. These interpretations describe conditional statistical relationships rather than causal effects. The resulting models offer a way to study mortality under alternative environmental scenarios while retaining a connection to classical actuarial survival models.

entry.title: Generative Modeling via Nonlinear Schrödinger Bridges and Branching Diffusions

link.title: Generative Modeling via Nonlinear Schrödinger Bridges and Branching Diffusions

entry.content:
We propose a new generative modeling framework grounded in forward-backward partial differential equations (PDEs). These equations arise naturally in mean-field game (MFG) theory, and are closely related to nonlinear Schr"odinger systems. Our main contribution is to reinterpret this connection within the setting of generative modeling and to develop an efficient numerical methodology for its practical implementation. Specifically, we derive and characterize a nonlinear extension of the classical Schr"odinger bridge problem through a coupled system of PDEs, yielding a model we call SBNL (Schr"odinger Bridge NonLinear). To compute its solution, we design a simulation algorithm based on branching diffusions and the probabilistic representation of semilinear PDEs. The resulting method is embarrassingly parallel, scalable to high dimensions, and applicable to a broad class of nonlinear interaction functionals. We validate the approach through numerical experiments, including recovery of the classical Schr"odinger bridge, nonlinear extensions with convex penalties (Gross-Pitaevskii) as well as potential interaction terms, and high-dimensional generative tasks such as image synthesis on the MNIST and FFHQ human face dataset. Furthermore, the same framework embeds score-based generative modeling, diffusion models, and tractable gaussian Schr"odinger bridges.

entry.title: Geometric Algebra for Neural Networks: A Survey

link.title: Geometric Algebra for Neural Networks: A Survey

entry.content:
Geometric algebra (GA) unifies geometric primitives and transformations in a single algebraic framework. Neural networks designed around this framework often represent features as multivectors and constrain layer operations to respect the algebraic structure, enabling principled treatment of geometric transformations and, in many cases, built-in equivariance. This survey reviews geometric algebra neural networks, including their building blocks, equivariant properties, application domains, empirical performance, and software support. We provide an algebra-selection guide, an empirical comparison of GA-based and other equivariant architectures, and a failure-mode analysis covering training pathologies, deployment constraints, and performance limitations. Across the surveyed literature, the strongest evidence for GA-based architectures appears in settings with explicit geometric symmetries and heterogeneous geometric entities; evidence for broader advantages in parameter efficiency, interpretability, and dense prediction is comparatively limited and uneven. We therefore conclude that geometric algebra neural networks are not universally superior to well-tuned non-GA equivariant baselines, and outline open problems in algebra selection, numerical stability, scalable implementation, and reproducible evaluation.

entry.title: Hierarchical Exponential-Gaussian Mixtures for Watch-Time Distribution Prediction

link.title: Hierarchical Exponential-Gaussian Mixtures for Watch-Time Distribution Prediction

entry.content:
Accurate watch-time (WT) prediction is an important requirement for short-video recommendations. Yet WT distributions are near-zero-inflated, long-tailed and multimodal. The recent Exponential-Gaussian Mixture Network (EGMN) models the full conditional WT distribution rather than a single point estimate and achieves state-of-the-art performance. Our large-scale reproduction study reveals that EGMN is vulnerable to variance collapse, component redundancy, and inactive components. We propose a Hierarchical Exponential-Gaussian Mixture (HEGM) model that addresses these failure modes through a hierarchical skip-watch decomposition, structured initialization, removal of the forced Gaussian shift and entropy regularizer and optional KL-based variance regularization for over-parameterized mixtures. Across large-scale industrial and public datasets, under a fixed-backbone head-replacement protocol, HEGM improves ranking accuracy and threshold-event prediction over reproducible lightweight baselines, while maintaining competitive point-estimation accuracy and substantially improving mixture stability and interpretability. A 1.5-month production A/B test confirms statistically significant engagement lifts. Our code and models are publicly released at https://github.com/rw404/HEGM.

entry.title: Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Survey Weighting: Local Equivalent Weights in Structured Populations

link.title: Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Survey Weighting: Local Equivalent Weights in Structured Populations

entry.content:
Regression-based survey weighting connects model-based population estimation with design-based inference through equivalent weights. For nonlinear models, equivalent weights can be defined locally through the sensitivity of a poststratified population estimator. However, conventional regression models may inadequately capture nonlinear relationships and complex interactions across sparse poststratification cells. We develop a survey-weighting framework based on hierarchical Gaussian process (HGP) regression, combining structured group-level effects with kernel-based smoothing to share information across related cells. We derive Gaussian posterior prediction formulas that exploit the structured covariance representation to reduce computational costs. We also establish a uniform convergence result for the posterior predictive mean under stated regularity conditions and construct local equivalent weights by matching the first-order sensitivity of a plug-in poststratified estimand to that of a weighted average of fitted response means, with both derivatives taken with respect to the latent mean-scale vector. Simulations show that HGP achieves lower population-weighted prediction error under nonparametric structure, whereas logistic regression performs well under correct parametric specification. Additional analyses examine sample size, frame coverage, subgroup prediction, and population-mean agreement. An application to the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study illustrates the method. Overall, this work extends local equivalent-weight construction to nonparametric modeling and provides a computational framework and conditional theoretical results for survey weighting in structured, sparse populations.

entry.title: How Do DiTs Denoise? An Aggregator-Predictor View of Attention and MLPs

link.title: How Do DiTs Denoise? An Aggregator-Predictor View of Attention and MLPs

entry.content:
How do diffusion transformers (DiTs) represent image content and learn rules for reusing it to generalize? We develop an aggregator–predictor view of DiTs as input-adaptive local denoisers, in which context aggregation and patch prediction provide functional roles for interpreting attention and MLPs. We first establish that, for Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) priors, the global Bayes denoiser can be approximated using only a subset of context patches, with error decaying exponentially in context radius. We further show that patchwise linear denoisers, often invoked to explain diffusion generalization, recover the empirical local denoiser with sufficiently informative aggregation. Within this view, AdaLN-modulated attention naturally parameterizes an input- and noise-dependent aggregator, while the MLP admits a learned key–value representation for tokenwise patch prediction. Our experiments support this view. DiTs trained on real images exhibit noise-dependent denoising contexts resembling those in the analytic GMRF setting, while attention mass exhibits a qualitatively corresponding broadening pattern. In a controlled CelebA64 study, shared-memory patch predictors used in place of DiT MLPs achieve competitive denoising and generative performance. Finally, cross-dataset component transplantation reveals compatibility patterns consistent with the proposed roles of QK in spatial weighting, VO in feature transport, and MLPs in patch prediction. Together, these results provide a component-level account of DiT denoising and motivate architecture-specific fine-tuning and controlled intervention.

entry.title: Interdomain Attention: Beyond Token-Level Key-Value Memory

link.title: Interdomain Attention: Beyond Token-Level Key-Value Memory

entry.content:
Softmax attention-based transformers and recurrent memory-based models (e.g., state space models (SSMs)) form the foundation of modern sequence models. Hybrid architectures aim to combine the expressivity from attention and the computational efficiency from recurrent memory, yet so far common practices simply stack both attention and recurrent layers. We propose Interdomain Attention (IA) as a novel hybrid attention architecture that mixes attention and recurrent memory in the same layer. Motivated by a kernel regression view of softmax attention, IA compresses values and kernel features of keys into a recurrent memory parameterized by an SSM. Then IA approximates dot-product attention by implicitly reconstructing the attention matrix and values from memory states; importantly this construction maintains SSM’s computational efficiency advantage. We demonstrate IA’s efficacy by designing and pre-training IA network architectures, where ablation studies identify attention-like readout as the primary source of gain over SSMs. Across 125M-1.3B models pre-trained on text data, IA improves over an S4D baseline at matched memory size. It also outperforms softmax attention-based Transformer in perplexity and accuracy on common-sense reasoning tasks. Based on Caduceus backbone, IA matches or outperforms the original SSM-based architecture in both perplexity and downstream tasks on genomic data.

entry.title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models

link.title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models

entry.content:
Reward guidance methods sample an exponential tilt of a base density using a diffusion model trained with only samples from the base distribution. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube ${-1,1}^{d}$, the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term.

entry.title: Is In-Context Reinforcement Learning A Posterior Sampler? An Empirical Study

link.title: Is In-Context Reinforcement Learning A Posterior Sampler? An Empirical Study

entry.content:
In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) exploits the impressive in-context learning ability of large language models to zero-shot generalize to new, unseen tasks at inference time without any parameter updates. Among many approaches, the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) is particularly appealing for its theoretical grounding: under idealized assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, DPT can perform Bayesian posterior sampling. Whether this characterization survives in practice remains open. Therefore, we ask: \textit{is ICRL, specifically DPT and our proposed DPT variants, a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice?} To approach this question, we establish two necessary conditions that a Bayesian posterior sampler must satisfy: \textit{sufficient-statistic invariance} and the \textit{martingale property}. We then construct statistical hypothesis tests to statistically assess if practically-trained ICRL models satisfy these conditions. Applying these tests in Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandit settings, we find that both conditions are consistently violated, suggesting that ICRL may not behave as Bayesian posterior samplers in practice. Beyond this negative result, our tests provide a principled toolkit for testing the Bayesian behavior of ICRL.

entry.title: Learning Checklists to Reduce Lottery Effects in Scientific Peer Review

link.title: Learning Checklists to Reduce Lottery Effects in Scientific Peer Review

entry.content:
Reviewer lottery error describes error due to a small set of peer reviews attending to only some of the issues with a paper that a larger pool of eligible reviewers would raise. We show this error can be reduced by surfacing a checklist of criticisms learned from a historical review corpus. Our approach generates a tree of checklists representing coarsenings of the atomic review claim space, then selects the coarsening that maximizes a theoretically-motivated measure of correlated agreement among reviewers. We realize this approach with an LLM-assisted pipeline and test it on NeurIPS 2021 and ICLR 2022 review data. In simulated review with LLM reviewers, the learned checklist reduces the mean squared error (MSE) of a three reviewer committee by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR, and on both venues the checklist with the highest correlated agreement has the lowest error for committees of three or more. In a human study with 20 participants, the learned NeurIPS checklist lowers the MSE of a paper ranking, measured against the NeurIPS 2021 order, from 0.48 to 0.22.

entry.title: Learning reshapes power-law anisotropy in internal representations

link.title: Learning reshapes power-law anisotropy in internal representations

entry.content:
Power-law anisotropy in internal representations has been observed across a wide range of biological and artificial neural systems, from state-of-the-art language models to the mouse cerebral cortex. This anisotropy is a key geometric property of high-dimensional information processing and underlies a variety of theoretical analyses. However, the mechanism by which it emerges from input structure and task-driven learning has remained unclear. Here, we characterize this formation process by exactly solving the learning dynamics of a wide two-layer linear neural network in a teacher–student setting with power-law input and teacher structures. We show that, in the feature-learning regime, the local power-law exponent of the internal-representation spectrum evolves nonmonotonically over the course of training and exhibits up to four distinct asymptotic regimes across modes and training times. By contrast, in the lazy regime, the exponent remains essentially unchanged. We further demonstrate numerically that similar exponent dynamics arise in more realistic nonlinear networks. Together, these results suggest a general mechanism by which the dynamic interaction between input statistics and task structure gives rise to power-law internal representations.

entry.title: Lifting PCA in the Wasserstein Space

link.title: Lifting PCA in the Wasserstein Space

entry.content:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a fundamental tool for statistical dimension reduction, yet no canonical extension to distribution-valued data has emerged within the framework of optimal transport. While Wasserstein barycenters and Wasserstein least-squares regression provide canonical liftings of Euclidean averaging and linear regression in the Wasserstein space, an analogous principle for PCA has remained unexplored. In this paper, we introduce Lifted PCA, a canonical extension of Euclidean PCA to Wasserstein space, obtained through the framework of lifting functionals in the space of probability measures by convex extension. Starting from the classical variational formulations of PCA on the Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds, we derive two equivalent minimization problems over probability measures supported on these manifolds that correspond to Wasserstein barycenters with generalized costs. We establish an exact analogue of the equivalence between the Stiefel and Grassmann formulations of Euclidean PCA, preserving PCA’s original variational structure under lifting. We further derive dual formulations and optimality conditions, and establish equivalences with multimarginal optimal transport and matching-for-teams problems. We also establish statistical consistency for empirical estimators and develop computational algorithms based on the Wasserstein barycenter formulation over the Stiefel manifold. Whereas Euclidean PCA summarizes vectors through projections onto an optimal low-dimensional linear subspace, Lifted PCA summarizes probability distributions through an optimal probability measure supported on multiple low-dimensional subspaces. Numerical experiments on distributional datasets illustrate the practical performance of the proposed methodology and its benefits for distributional data analysis.

entry.title: Mastering Model Fit: Applications of the InterModel Vigorish for Interpretable Machine Learning

link.title: Mastering Model Fit: Applications of the InterModel Vigorish for Interpretable Machine Learning

entry.content:
Accuracy alone gives little information about which features or model components improve probabilistic fit, which outcomes benefit, or how fit changes during training. We introduce the InterModel Vigorish (IMV) into the Machine Intelligence space in order to express differences in fit as an expected betting advantage over a reference model. SHAP-IMV attributes gains to features through Shapley-weighted subset comparisons, Multi-IMV evaluates one-vs-rest and pairwise class discrimination, and Ablate-IMV assesses architectural components and feature groups by ablation. We evaluate these applications over ten random seeds using tabular data, images, sensor sequences, and graphs. Feature rankings vary across estimators. High one-vs-rest accuracy can accompany negligible improvement over a null, while ablation can preserve or improve fit under a fixed training budget. On six graph-classification benchmarks, we time-profile IMV over 200 training epochs, reporting seed means and ranges. The open-source imvpy library and accompanying notebooks provide code to replicate our work and to use the IMV more widely.

entry.title: Memorizing Long-tail Data Can Help Generalization Through Composition

link.title: Memorizing Long-tail Data Can Help Generalization Through Composition

entry.content:
Deep learning has led researchers to rethink the relationship between memorization and generalization. In many settings, memorization does not hurt generalization due to implicit regularization and may help by memorizing long-tailed examples. In this paper, we consider the synergy between memorization and simple composition – the ability to make correct prediction on a combination of long-tailed features. Theoretically, we show that for a linear setting, memorization together with composition can help the model make correct predictions on rare test examples that require a combination of long-tailed features, even if such combinations were never observed in the training data. Experiments on neural network architecture on simple data show that the theoretical insight extends beyond the linear setting, and we further observe that the composition capability of the model depends on its architecture.

entry.title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning

link.title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning

entry.content:
Training generative models on synthetic data causes loss of diversity and a decrease in performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. We study this degeneration spectrally in a controlled Markov setting. The eigenvalue spectrum of the learned transition operator offers a direct view of the process, since the subdominant eigenvalues set how fast the chain mixes and therefore how much of the state space it continues to explore. We find that sampling at temperature $T_s < 1$ acts on the operator like repeated sharpening, pushing it toward a deterministic system: the subdominant eigenvalues approach the unit circle and the spectral gap narrows. When $T_s < 1$, even data accumulation does not appear to arrest this drift. We then analyze Dreaming Learning, a regulariser that, in parallel with regular training, adds a loss term on the model’s own samples drawn at a raised temperature $T_d > 1$. Because high-temperature samples flatten the predicted distribution, training on them keeps the entries of the learned operator from becoming vanishingly small, which in turn keeps the eigenvalues bounded away from the unit circle. Measurements of the spectra over 5000 generations are consistent with this picture, and the mitigation effect persists in more complex settings such as LSTM language models and a 124M-parameter GPT-2.

entry.title: Model-agnostic information transfer and fusion for classification with label noise

link.title: Model-agnostic information transfer and fusion for classification with label noise

entry.content:
Label noise presents a fundamental challenge in modern machine learning, especially when large-scale datasets are generated via automated processes. An increasingly common and important data paradigm, particularly in domains like medical imaging, involves learning from a large dataset with coarse, noisy labels supplemented by a small, expert-verified, clean dataset. This setting constitutes a typical information transfer and fusion problem. However, the significant distribution shift between the noisy and clean data violates the core overall parametric similarity assumptions of existing statistical transfer learning methods, while their reliance on parametric models is ill-suited for complex data like images. To address these limitations, this paper develops a generic model-agnostic nonparametric framework for classification with label noise, which applies to a broad class of classifiers. Our approach leverages the small clean dataset to ``purify’’ the large noisy one and carefully manages the remaining ambiguous samples. This framework is underpinned by a rigorous statistical theory. Its empirical performance is demonstrated through simulations and a real-world application to medical image analysis for pneumonia diagnosis.

entry.title: Multi-Label Sentiment Analysis on 100 Languages with Dynamic Weighting for Label Imbalance

link.title: Multi-Label Sentiment Analysis on 100 Languages with Dynamic Weighting for Label Imbalance

entry.content:
We investigate cross-lingual sentiment analysis, which has attracted significant attention due to its applications in various areas including market research, politics and social sciences. In particular, we introduce a sentiment analysis framework in multi-label setting as it obeys Plutchik’s wheel of emotions. We introduce a novel dynamic weighting method that balances the contribution from each class during training, unlike previous static weighting methods that assign non-changing weights based on their class frequency. Moreover, we adapt the focal loss that favors harder instances from single-label object recognition literature to our multi-label setting. Furthermore, we derive a method to choose optimal class-specific thresholds that maximize the macro-f1 score in linear time complexity. Through an extensive set of experiments, we show that our method obtains the state-of-the-art performance in 7 of 9 metrics in 3 different languages using a single model compared to the common baselines and the best-performing methods in the SemEval competition. We publicly share our code for our model, which can perform sentiment analysis in 100 languages, to facilitate further research.

entry.title: Near Minimax Rate for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning

link.title: Near Minimax Rate for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning

entry.content:
In this paper, we study quantile distributional policy evaluation, where the return distribution under a given policy is approximated by the quantile Bellman fixed point $\bm\eta_m$. We investigate the statistical accuracy of estimating $\bm\eta_m$ across quantile resolutions under Wasserstein distances. Assuming access to a generative model, we construct a quantile fixed point estimator $\bm\eta_m^{(n)}$ from an empirical Markov decision process and establish non-asymptotic error bounds under Wasserstein distances. When reward densities are uniformly bounded away from zero, we obtain a root-$n$ high-probability bound simultaneously over all resolutions $m$ and all Wasserstein orders $1\le p\le\infty$. When reward densities vanish at the support endpoints, we show that continuity and endpoint monotonicity suffice to preserve the same resolution-independent rate for $1\le p\le2$. For $p>2$, we establish a root-$n$ bound with coefficient $m^{1/2-1/p}$, together with a slower, resolution-independent $n^{-1/p}$ bound for every finite $p>2$. We further obtain resolution-independent $W_\infty$ consistency governed by the continuity modulus of reward quantile functions. To investigate the sharpness of these bounds, we characterize the exact local asymptotic minimax risk at each fixed resolution as the expected Wasserstein-coordinate norm of the efficient Gaussian limit and prove that our estimator attains it. We then examine the resolution dependence of this optimal local risk. A regular one-state instance has resolution-independent local risk constants, whereas a single endpoint-vanishing two-state instance exhibits growth of order $m^{1/2-1/p}$, up to logarithmic factors along a resolution subsequence, for every $p>2$.

entry.title: Network Cross-Validation and Model Selection via Subsampling

link.title: Network Cross-Validation and Model Selection via Subsampling

entry.content:
Complex and larger networks are becoming increasingly prevalent in scientific applications in various domains. Although a number of models and methods exist for such networks, cross-validation on networks remains challenging due to the unique structure of network data. In this paper, we propose a general cross-validation procedure called NETCROP (NETwork CRoss-Validation using Overlapping Partitions). The key idea is to divide the original network into multiple subnetworks with a shared overlap part, producing training sets consisting of the subnetworks and a test set with the node pairs between the subnetworks. This train-test split provides the basis for a network cross-validation procedure that can be applied on a wide range of model selection and parameter tuning problems for networks. The method is computationally efficient for large networks as it uses smaller subnetworks for the training step. We provide methodological details and theoretical guarantees for several model selection and parameter tuning tasks using NETCROP. Numerical results demonstrate that NETCROP performs accurate cross-validation on a diverse set of network model selection and parameter tuning problems. The results also indicate that NETCROP is computationally much faster while being often more accurate than the existing methods for network cross-validation.

entry.title: One Act, Many Masks: Effect-Marginal Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Agents

link.title: One Act, Many Masks: Effect-Marginal Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Agents

entry.content:
Recent advances in multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) have substantially improved the performance of LLM agents on complex, long-horizon interactive tasks. However, despite progress in fine-grained credit assignment, policy optimization still applies these learning signals through response-specific probability ratios. Different textual responses can induce the same executable effect, yet credit differences arising from subsequent outcomes remain tied to their individual textual realizations. We identify this mismatch as credit-update misalignment. Our analysis reveals that credit-text pairing directly shapes policy-update directions, even when the policy context and executable effect are held fixed. Motivated by this finding, we propose Effect-Marginal Policy Optimization (EMPO), which aligns policy optimization with execution-level equivalence through an effect-level surrogate that couples updates across alternative textual realizations. EMPO preserves the original credit signals, integrates with both trajectory-level and step-level credit estimators, and requires no additional critics or rollouts. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Sokoban show that EMPO outperforms strong baselines in both task performance and learning efficiency.

entry.title: Online Augmented Plug-in Inference for Multi-group Fair Prediction

link.title: Online Augmented Plug-in Inference for Multi-group Fair Prediction

entry.content:
Fairness regularization changes both a prediction rule and its sampling uncertainty. We develop online inference for classifiers trained with a covariance penalty on group mean decision scores, a tractable proxy for demographic parity. The framework includes logistic regression and smoothed support-vector machines, with linear regression as a special case targeting equality of group mean predictions. The inferential challenge arises because the fairness operator is estimated from the same stream used to update the predictor. Each observation contributes to its current loss gradient and to subsequent penalty estimates, creating an additional first-order fluctuation in the Polyak–Ruppert average. We derive an asymptotic expansion with harmonic reuse weights and an augmented covariance incorporating score variation, operator variation, and their dependence. Exact fixed-memory recursions yield a consistent covariance estimator and asymptotically valid confidence intervals for the penalized coefficients. Simulation studies assess coverage and interval contraction. Adult-income classification and IPUMS wage regression illustrate coefficient uncertainty and fairness–utility trade-offs, with classification demographic parity evaluated separately through threshold decisions.

entry.title: Optimally Emulating Smooth Functions for Bayesian Analyses

link.title: Optimally Emulating Smooth Functions for Bayesian Analyses

entry.content:
For Bayesian analyses aimed at constraining the parameter space of computationally expensive models by comparison with heterogeneous data sets, model emulators play a pivotal role. Model emulators enable searches through high-dimensional parameter spaces, searches which might otherwise require millions of full model runs. Here, an emulation strategy is presented based on the assumption that the model output can be well described by a polynomial expansion with all terms being independent of one another and with higher order terms being given decreasing weights according to a convergence parameter. It is found that if the expansion’s form is constrained to being invariant to rotation and translation of the parameter space that the polynomial form becomes equivalent to that of a Gaussian process emulator using a correlation kernel with a Gaussian form. In the limit that the function is smooth, quantified by a convergence parameter, $\Lambda$, it is found that rather few training points are required to reproduce the full model and provide a good estimate of its uncertainty. An accuracy metric is defined based on an average of the expected uncertainty over the prior before training data are actually gathered. Analytic expressions for the expected accuracy are provided based solely on an expected value of $\Lambda$ and the location of the training points. This enables a tenable optimized placement of training points, which is shown to be significantly superior to random placement or that from Latin hyper-cube sampling. Examples of optimized placement are provided, and the accuracy is studied as a function of various variables, such as the number of model parameters, the number of training points, and the convergence parameter.

entry.title: Optimized Conformal Selection: Powerful Selective Inference After Data-Dependent Score Construction

link.title: Optimized Conformal Selection: Powerful Selective Inference After Data-Dependent Score Construction

entry.content:
We study data-driven score construction in conformal selection, which uses conformal p-values and multiple testing to select “interesting” instances with large unobserved labels from a pool of unlabeled data, while controlling the FDR in finite sample. While existing solutions require the score function to be constructed independent of the calibration and test data, it is desirable to select or construct powerful conformity score in a data-driven manner and to leverage all labeled data for score training when presented with many score choices and limited labeled data. We propose Optimized Conformal Selection (OptCS), a general framework that allows valid multiple testing after flexible data-driven score construction. We introduce general conditions under which OptCS constructs valid conformal p-values despite substantial data reuse and handles complex p-value dependencies to maintain finite-sample FDR control. We instantiate this general recipe to propose three FDR-controlling procedures, each optimizing the models differently: (i) selecting a powerful score function among multiple candidates, (ii) training the score with all labeled data without sample splitting, and (iii) combining full-sample training and model selection. We demonstrate the efficacy of our methods via simulation studies and real applications in drug discovery and large language models.

entry.title: Perceived vertical and eye level as one orientation process: a closed-form account of the Li-Matin combination rules for egocentric space

link.title: Perceived vertical and eye level as one orientation process: a closed-form account of the Li-Matin combination rules for egocentric space

entry.content:
Li and Matin (2005a, 2005b) reported three regularities of the induced visually-perceived vertical (VPV), the direction judged upright. For small tilts, a peripheral line shifts it nearly linearly with tilt, two lines combine nearly linearly, and mirror-image tilts cancel. Each line votes at twice its angle, weighted by its strength. The votes’ vector sum $c_1$ is the first circular moment of the doubled angles; half its angle, $\phi=\tfrac12\arg c_1$, is the induced vertical, a stimulus axis, not the judged upright. This is the orientation order-parameter model (PLUMB). We prove that $c_1$ is, up to a constant factor, the only additive summary of axes (lines without arrowheads) that scales with line strength and turns twice as far as the field rotates. With Li and Matin’s own length gain and no per-configuration fit, the model matches their multiline coefficients in-sample. Their data rule out complete summation but not simple averaging for long lines. But a line’s effect is fourfold (period $90^\circ$): it reverses past $45^\circ$ (Li and Matin, 2005a; Vingerhoets et al., 2009), and near-horizontal lines shift VPV as near-vertical ones do, which $c_1$ forbids. In a two-harmonic fit to Li and Matin’s data, $c_1$ carries an estimated 2–4% of a near-vertical line’s slope and a fourfold term the rest. To first order in tilt, for near-vertical segments, the readout equals the committee rule Shavit, Li, and Matin (2026) fit to eight line-array experiments, with its drives read as concentrations. If the half-fields’ signals are read as sum and difference, perceived eye level (VPEL) is the difference, recovering Shavit, Li, and Matin’s (2013) reversed integration rules; a fourfold term gives the same signals, so this does not single out $c_1$. Re-analysed data (30 observers) show the predicted signs and nulls, an internal check only; the cross-field gain is fitted.

entry.title: Phase Transitions in Collective Damage of Civil Structures under Natural Hazards

link.title: Phase Transitions in Collective Damage of Civil Structures under Natural Hazards

entry.content:
The fate of cities under natural hazards depends not only on hazard intensity but also on the coupling of structural damage, a collective process that remains poorly understood. Here we show that urban structural damage exhibits phase-transition phenomena. As hazard intensity increases, the system can shift abruptly from a largely safe to a largely damaged state, analogous to a discontinuous phase transition in statistical physics. Higher diversity in the building portfolio smooths this transition, but multiscale damage clustering traps the system in a highly volatile regime that suppresses the emergence of predictable Gaussian statistics. The observed phenomenological patterns are interpreted through an effective random-field Ising model, with its key parameters translated into tangible engineering variables such as hazard demand, structural diversity, and modeling uncertainty. These insights establish a phase-aware description of collective damage, revealing that common engineering simplifications can distort the inherent phase of real urban portfolios. Critically, such phase distortions can substantially bias hazard loss estimates, producing relative errors of up to 50% in exceedance probabilities under moderate earthquakes—equivalent to a several-fold gap in anticipated repair costs. The phase-aware description turns the collective behavior of civil infrastructure damage into actionable diagnostics for urban risk assessment and planning.

entry.title: Population Neuroscience 3.0: Bridging large-N and small-N paradigms in brain-wide association studies

link.title: Population Neuroscience 3.0: Bridging large-N and small-N paradigms in brain-wide association studies

entry.content:
Brain-wide association studies (BWAS) leveraging large datasets, have led to divergent and sometimes opposing views on research practices and priorities. The debates span multiple dimensions, including large-N vs.\ small-N sampling, cross-sectional vs.\ longitudinal, observational vs.\ interventional/causal, population generalizability vs.\ individual specificity, data-driven vs.\ hypothesis-driven, prediction-oriented vs.\ explanation-oriented, and molecular/cellular vs.\ systems-level. entry.title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies

link.title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies

entry.content:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.

entry.title: Privacy Accounting for Empirical Denoisers

link.title: Privacy Accounting for Empirical Denoisers

entry.content:
Diffusion models have emerged as the foundation of modern generative systems, yet their high memorization capacity raises privacy concerns. While differentially private (DP) training provides formal guarantees, it comes at a cost in sample quality. In this work, we study a complementary question: how much privacy loss is incurred during the sampling process itself? Directly analyzing modern neural denoisers is challenging because their sensitivity to a single training example is generally intractable. To overcome this challenge, we construct and analyze a clipped privacy-accountable empirical denoiser, a training-free estimator of the Bayes-optimal denoiser, whose per-step sensitivity can be computed explicitly, allowing each denoising step to be a Gaussian mechanism. This perspective enables privacy accounting under Gaussian DP when each training example contributes to each denoising step, and under $f$-DP trade-off functions when each generated sample uses a single randomly subsampled block of the training data. We report every $(\varepsilon, \delta)$ guarantee as a certified upper bound from a privacy loss distribution accountant, and use a cumulant-based Edgeworth approximation as a fast diagnostic, characterizing where it is reliable and where it becomes anti-conservative. We also analyze the privacy loss along the denoising trajectory and show that it grows steeply near the critical window in which semantic content is formed. This observation motivates hybrid samplers that use the private empirical denoiser through the formative steps where it remains a faithful proxy for the neural denoiser, then switch to a public neural denoiser for the remaining refinement. Our results on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-64 show that the privacy of diffusion models depends not only on the training procedure, but also on sampling-time design choices such as subsampling, stopping time, and hybrid denoising.

entry.title: Private Online Prediction from Experts with Small Losses

link.title: Private Online Prediction from Experts with Small Losses

entry.content:
We consider online prediction from experts, a fundamental problem in machine learning, under differential privacy constraints. Existing private algorithms achieve near-optimal regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the time horizon. However, this bound becomes suboptimal when $L^\star$, the cumulative loss of the best expert, is significantly less than $T$. In this work, we present the first differentially private algorithm with regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{L^\star})$, offering a substantial improvement in the low-loss regime. Our regret bound matches the non-private lower bound up to poly-logarithmic factors for constant privacy parameters, demonstrating that privacy incurs only a small cost in this setting. Our result assumes that the input sequence is oblivious, i.e., it is fixed in advance and independent of the algorithm’s outputs. We also prove that an $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{T})$ regret is inevitable for adaptively generated inputs, even when $L^\star = 0$.

entry.title: Proximal Balancing for Causal Effect Estimation under Unmeasured Confounding

link.title: Proximal Balancing for Causal Effect Estimation under Unmeasured Confounding

entry.content:
Estimating causal effects from observational data is central to science and policy, but the effects are not identified when confounders are unmeasured. Proximal causal inference addresses this problem with proxies of the unmeasured confounders. However, existing proxy-based approaches either designate proxy roles and solve an inverse problem, which is ill-posed and hard to estimate with high-dimensional proxies, or use a latent-variable model, which assumes that the learned latent variable matches the hidden confounder and leaves bias when it does not. To address these challenges, we introduce proximal balancing. It carries the classical idea of covariate balancing to confounders that are observed only through proxies: it learns a low-dimensional summary of the covariates and proxies that makes the treatment groups comparable, and then adjusts for this summary. It needs no designated proxy roles, inverse problem, or latent model. We give identification theory, finite-sample guarantees, and a practical algorithm, PROBE. We demonstrate the method on low-dimensional, high-dimensional, and image proxies and on real-world data.

entry.title: Rare-Feature-Adaptive Subsampling for Big Data Regression

link.title: Rare-Feature-Adaptive Subsampling for Big Data Regression

entry.content:
Rare binary features cause instability and slow convergence in regression. Subsampling massive datasets may discard observations carrying rare-feature information. We show that rare-feature coefficient convergence rates depend on feature prevalence and the inclusion probabilities assigned to rare observations. This finding motivates subsampling designs that adapt sampling probabilities to feature rarity. We first study optimal rare-census designs, which extend the negative subsampling approach by retaining every rare observation. However, they may face practical constraints. We then propose a computationally efficient rarity-adaptive L-optimal design that incorporates inverse prevalence scaling. Because implementing optimal designs requires pilot estimates whose quality depends on adequate representation of rare features, we propose a balanced design, a one-step rarity-adaptive design based only on binary features. It can be used alone, as a pilot, or combined with designs targeting other objectives. For implementation in two stages, we develop a union-sample estimator that reuses pilot observations while accounting for sample overlap and establish its asymptotic normality. Simulations and applications show improved stability and estimation efficiency over existing methods. One application evaluates designs that jointly protect rare outcomes and rare features.

entry.title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning

link.title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning

entry.content:
RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO’s credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.

entry.title: Residual-Based Causal Discovery via Pretrained In-Context Quantile Regression

link.title: Residual-Based Causal Discovery via Pretrained In-Context Quantile Regression

entry.content:
Residual-based causal discovery assumes that each variable is generated from its parents and an independent noise source. It estimates this noise and tests its independence from candidate causes. For identifiable functions such as additive-noise models (ANMs) and the broader class of location-scale noise models (LSNMs), this principle identifies the causal direction, as only the causal model admits this independence. Existing LSNM methods rely on parametric assumptions to obtain standardized residuals, risking model misspecification. In contrast, the RESIT-framework allows for nonparametric estimation of residuals to iteratively identify sink nodes, but was proposed for ANMs. To close this gap, we propose Loscar, an extension of RESIT to LSNMs that estimates the conditional mean and scale via quantile regression, enabling pretrained tabular foundation models as plug-in estimators. We compare it with a feasible generalized least squares (FGLS) variant, which is consistent given suitable basis functions. Across bivariate and multivariate causal-discovery benchmarks, in-context quantile regression substantially outperforms FGLS with flexible function classes, particularly for multivariate causes.

entry.title: Schrödinger-Bass Bridge Barycenter Models for Measure-Valued Data

link.title: Schrödinger-Bass Bridge Barycenter Models for Measure-Valued Data

entry.content:
Barycenter models, based on stochastic and deterministic optimal transport bridges between probability measures, have proven to be useful for supervised and unsupervised learning for (probability) measure-valued data. In this paper, we utilize the directional asymmetry and dual drift-diffusion control arising in the recently proposed Schr"odinger-Bass Bridge (SBB) between two measures, and propose \textit{SBB-encoder}, \textit{SBB-decoder}, \textit{SBB-symmetric}, and \textit{SBB-Markovian} barycenter models. For each of these novel models, our first theoretical result establishes the existence of the SBB-barycenter under mild assumptions. Our second theoretical result characterizes the decoder SBB-barycenter of Gaussians where we show that for Gaussian input measures, the decoder formulation admits a Gaussian minimizer, reducing barycenter computation to a finite-dimensional optimization and yielding a compact algorithm. For general input measures, we derive a hybrid Wasserstein gradient particle descent scheme for all four formulations using the SBB dual representation. Finally, we utilize these algorithms for solving distributional-inverse/interpolation problems arising in the context of spatial images and single-cell RNA sequencing data, where we show that the SBB-decoder and Markovian barycenter allow us to interpolate between successive time points. Results show that our method outperforms existing barycenter models for measure interpolation and inference.

entry.title: Sequential Entropic Optimal Transport for Bayesian Inverse Problems via Multilevel Monte Carlo

link.title: Sequential Entropic Optimal Transport for Bayesian Inverse Problems via Multilevel Monte Carlo

entry.content:
We consider the problem of Bayesian estimation associated to inverse problems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). In most cases of practical interest, one must use numerical solvers to implement computational methods based on Monte Carlo methods. This inevitably leads to an adaptation of multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) methods to reduce computational efforts to achieve a pre-specified mean square error (MSE). MLMC is based on sampling coupled versions of Bayesian posteriors associated to increasingly precise numerical solves of the PDE. In this article we present a novel method to implement MLMC based upon sequential entropic optimal transport couplings learned with light Schr"odinger bridges, and correct the transport with Metropolis–Hastings steps that preserve the pairing. We bound the mean square error associated to a version of our new estimation method and show, for an elliptic inverse problem, that to achieve a MSE of $\mathcal{O}(\delta^2)$ ($\delta >0$) one can have an optimal cost of $\mathcal{O}(\delta^{-2})$. The results feature explicit bounds on the effect of the fitted transport and of the Metropolis–Hastings correction. From a numerical perspective, on elliptic, Darcy-flow and Navier-Stokes problems, the method reduces the variance of the most precise solver by a factor of five to ten and is faster than multilevel sequential Monte Carlo [arXiv:1503.07259] at tight accuracies.

entry.title: Sequential sparse Gaussian process quantile regression

link.title: Sequential sparse Gaussian process quantile regression

entry.content:
Quantile regression aims to estimate the conditional quantiles of a response variable from observed data. In a Bayesian setting, Gaussian process quantile regression provides uncertainty quantification but faces significant computational challenges due to the nonconjugacy of the asymmetric Laplace likelihood and the cost of posterior inference. We develop a sparse Gaussian process framework in which the quantile function is represented through a reduced set of inducing variables and posterior inference is performed using a Laplace approximation. A decomposition of the predictive uncertainty into conditional-prior and posterior-induced variance components is then exploited to drive two complementary adaptive mechanisms: inducing-input infilling and data acquisition. These mechanisms are combined within a sequential algorithm that allocates computational effort toward the dominant source of predictive uncertainty and adaptively controls model complexity. Numerical experiments on benchmark problems demonstrate the accuracy of the Laplace approximation, the benefits of variance-based inducing-input placement, and the effectiveness of the proposed sequential enrichment strategy compared with predefined data-acquisition strategies. The method is finally applied to ship seakeeping under forecast uncertainty, where it outperforms a replication-based counterpart from the literature under limited simulation budgets.

entry.title: Silent Alignment in Two-Layer Linear Networks: A High-Dimensional Perspective

link.title: Silent Alignment in Two-Layer Linear Networks: A High-Dimensional Perspective

entry.content:
We study gradient flow in a two-layer linear network in the high-dimensional regime where the input, inner and output dimensions diverge proportionally. Under whitened inputs and isotropic imbalance, we combine a closed-form solution of the dynamics with prior random matrix theory results to derive a high-dimensional limit for the dynamics. Our method yields exact asymptotic spectral distributions for the weight matrices at all times and characterizes the evolution of the learned subspace. In the small-initialization limit, we identify a silent alignment phenomenon: the singular directions of the network align on an order-one timescale, while the singular values and empirical loss remain at their initial values. Visible learning occurs later, on a logarithmic timescale, as singular values progressively escape zero and the loss decreases. This phase is characterized by a saddle-to-saddle dynamics, which becomes a continuous process of spectral learning in the high-dimensional limit.

link.title: Simulation of warping processes with applications to temperature data

entry.content:
Curve registration plays a major role in functional data analysis by separating amplitude and phase variation through warping functions and the accurate simulation of warping processes is essential for developing statistical methods that properly account for phase variability in functional data. In this paper, we focus on the simulation of continuous warping processes with a prescribed expectation and a controllable variance. We study and compare three procedures, including two existing methods and a new algorithm based on randomized empirical cumulative distribution functions. For each approach, we provide an operational description and establish theoretical results for the first two moments of the simulated processes. A numerical study illustrates the theoretical findings and highlights the respective merits of the three methods. Finally, we present an application to the analysis of hourly temperature data spatially averaged over Canada, based on simulated realizations from a warping process estimated using spatially averaged temperature quantile functions.

entry.title: Structured Temporal Causality for Interpretable Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

link.title: Structured Temporal Causality for Interpretable Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

entry.content:
Real-world multivariate time series anomalies are rare and often unlabeled. Additionally, prevailing methods rely on increasingly complex architectures tuned to benchmarks, detecting only fragments of anomalous segments and overstating performance. In this paper, we introduce OracleAD, a simple and interpretable unsupervised framework for multivariate time series anomaly detection. OracleAD encodes each variable’s past sequence into a single causal embedding to jointly predict the present time point and reconstruct the input window, effectively modeling temporal dynamics. These embeddings then undergo a self-attention mechanism to project them into a shared latent space and capture spatial relationships. These relationships are not static, since they are modeled by a property that emerges from each variable’s temporal dynamics. The projected embeddings are aligned to a Stable Latent Structure (SLS) representing normal-state relationships. Anomalies are identified using a dual scoring mechanism based on prediction error and deviation from the SLS, enabling fine-grained anomaly diagnosis at each time point and across individual variables. Since any noticeable SLS deviation originates from embeddings that violate the learned temporal causality of normal data, OracleAD directly pinpoints the root-cause variables at the embedding level. OracleAD achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple real-world datasets and evaluation protocols, while remaining interpretable through SLS.

entry.title: Technical Report: Causal ANOVA Applied to COMPAS

link.title: Technical Report: Causal ANOVA Applied to COMPAS

entry.content:
This report applies Causal ANOVA to the COMPAS recidivism prediction dataset to study how demographic variables contribute to variation in two-year recidivism outcomes. Using a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to encode causal assumptions, we estimate counterfactual explainability scores for Race, Sex, and Age Category. We then examine whether the explanatory roles of Race and Sex change after conditioning on age group. The results suggest that Age Category explains the largest share of variation in the full causal model. After conditioning on age, Sex explainability is highest among younger defendants and declines with age, while Race explainability increases with age and is most pronounced among older defendants. As a complementary analysis, we use logistic regression models to interpret the demographic patterns suggested by the Causal ANOVA results. We provide a Python package of Causal ANOVA at https://github.com/devonxiong/causal-anova.

entry.title: Testing the statistical compatibility of data sets with a common prior

link.title: Testing the statistical compatibility of data sets with a common prior

entry.content:
The Parameter Goodness-of-fit (PG) test [hep-ph/0304176] offers a simple test statistic to study the compatibility of different data sets within a given theoretical model. In its original formulation it assumes that the data sets are statistically independent. We propose an extension of the PG test for the situation when some parameters of the model are constrained by an auxiliary data set called prior here. As the prior is imposed for all data sets, they are no longer statistically independent. We show that under the Gaussian approximation, the prior-constrained PG test statistic follows a generalised $\chi^2$ distribution, which can be used to obtain $p$-values in a straight-forward way. In the approximation of a strong prior constraint, the test converges towards the standard PG test for the unconstrained model parameters.

entry.title: The Limits of Post-Selection Generalization

link.title: The Limits of Post-Selection Generalization

entry.content:
While statistics and machine learning offer numerous methods for ensuring generalization, these methods often fail in the presence of adaptivity—the common practice in which the choice of analysis depends on previous interactions with the same dataset. A recent line of work has introduced powerful, general purpose algorithms that ensure post hoc generalization (also called robust or post-selection generalization), which says that, given the output of the algorithm, it is hard to find any statistic for which the data differs significantly from the population it came from. In this work we show several limitations on the power of algorithms satisfying post hoc generalization. First, we show a tight lower bound on the error of any algorithm that satisfies post hoc generalization and answers adaptively chosen statistical queries, showing a strong barrier to progress in post selection data analysis. Second, we show that post hoc generalization is not closed under composition, despite many examples of such algorithms exhibiting strong composition properties.

entry.title: The Predictive–Optimization Gap in GuanDan Self-Play

link.title: The Predictive–Optimization Gap in GuanDan Self-Play

entry.content:
Outcome-predictive signals are often treated as promising optimization targets in reinforcement learning, but predictive validity and optimization utility are different claims. We expose this distinction in GuanDan, a multi-round imperfect-information game in which the implication of a round outcome depends on the public match state. Held-out analysis shows that state–gain interactions provide incremental predictive value beyond a constant signed-gain effect, establishing that match progress is predictively meaningful. We then use changes in a frozen match-win predictor, $\Delta\Phi$, as a controlled round-level supervision intervention in a matched DanZero-style Monte Carlo self-play protocol. The intervention can succeed in an individual lineage: a selected progress-augmented checkpoint substantially outperforms its matched Baseline on a locked evaluation. Yet the method-level result reverses this impression: none of five preregistered replication seeds is positive, the pooled ten-seed interval includes zero, and across-iteration effects repeatedly change sign without a common late-stage advantage. These results identify a predictive–optimization gap: under the studied learner, a signal can describe outcome-relevant progress while failing to provide a reliably beneficial optimization direction.

entry.title: The Price of Current-Effect Inference in Nonstationary Multi-Armed Bandits

link.title: The Price of Current-Effect Inference in Nonstationary Multi-Armed Bandits

entry.content:
Adaptive experiments use bandit algorithms to favor interventions with higher expected rewards. However, decision-makers also require reliable inference on current treatment effects: differences between intervention and reference-arm mean rewards at the present time, rather than historical averages. These objectives conflict: reward maximization favors better interventions, whereas current-effect inference requires continued exploration of potentially suboptimal interventions as outcomes change over time. We characterize this tradeoff for $K$-arm bandits with H"older-smooth mean rewards of exponent $\beta\in(0,1]$ and constant $L$. Requiring high-probability simultaneous coverage of all current effects by confidence intervals of width at most $w$, we establish matching minimax bounds, up to logarithmic factors, on expected dynamic regret. Over horizon $T$, our algorithm TRACE (Tracking Rewards and Current Effects) achieves regret of order $\widetilde{O}_{\beta}\left(\sqrt{KT}+K^{\beta/(2\beta+1)}L^{1/(2\beta+1)}T^{(\beta+1)/(2\beta+1)}+Kw^{-2}(1+L^{1/\beta}w^{-1/\beta})\right)$, where the notation hides logarithms and constants depending only on $\beta$. This regret–precision tradeoff separates reward-learning regret from the cost of refreshing current-effect estimates, which remains unavoidable even when one arm is uniformly optimal. An empirical-Bernstein e-process extension adapts exploration to realized prediction errors while preserving worst-case guarantees. When within-block drift is negligible relative to sampling error, all observations, including reward-learning observations, can be reused for asymptotically normal pointwise inference and stronger local stationarity yields local asymptotic efficiency. Finally, we show that regret constraints can prevent honest adaptation to unknown smoothness and support our theory with extensive numerical experiments.

entry.title: The Sample Complexity of Multiple Change Point Identification under Bandit Feedback

link.title: The Sample Complexity of Multiple Change Point Identification under Bandit Feedback

entry.content:
We study multiple change point localization under bandit feedback. An unknown piecewise-constant function on a compact interval can be queried sequentially at adaptively chosen inputs, and each query returns a noisy evaluation of the function. The goal is to identify a prescribed number of discontinuities, known as change points, within a target precision $\eta$ and confidence level $1-\delta$, while using as few samples as possible. We propose an adaptive algorithm that first detects intervals likely to contain change points and then refines their locations to precision $\eta$. We establish non-asymptotic upper bounds on its sample budget, together with corresponding lower bounds. Prior work shows that jump magnitudes alone determine the asymptotic sample complexity as $\delta\to 0$. We reveal that this picture is incomplete beyond this regime. We demonstrate, both empirically and theoretically, that for general $\delta$ and $\eta$, the complexity is jointly governed by the jumps and the relative positions of the change points.

entry.title: The dynamic generalized covariance measure for conditional independence testing with nonstationary time series

link.title: The dynamic generalized covariance measure for conditional independence testing with nonstationary time series

entry.content:
Identifying relationships among stochastic processes is a core objective in many fields, such as economics. While the standard toolkit for multivariate time series analysis has many advantages, it can be difficult to capture nonlinear dynamics using linear vector autoregressive models. This difficulty has motivated the development of methods for causal discovery and variable selection for nonlinear time series, which routinely employ tests for conditional independence. In this paper, we introduce the first framework for conditional independence testing that works with a single realization of a nonstationary nonlinear process. The proposed test is designed to have power against alternatives in which the expected conditional covariance is non-zero for at least some times. We also discuss an approach for gaining power against a broader range of alternatives. The key technical ingredients of our framework are time-varying nonlinear regression, estimation of local long-run covariance matrices of products of error processes, and a distribution-uniform strong Gaussian approximation.

entry.title: The role of locality and weight sharing in convolutional neural networks

link.title: The role of locality and weight sharing in convolutional neural networks

entry.content:
The success of convolutional neural networks is often attributed to locality and weight sharing. However, how these two properties separately shape learning, and how their effects depend on the spatial correlations of natural images, remain poorly understood. We address these questions in a teacher-student model with a convolutional teacher acting on $P$ input positions with correlation $c$ between positions. We compare convolutional and locally connected students trained by online stochastic gradient descent, and derive ordinary differential equations that describe their dynamics exactly in the limit of large feature dimension $D$. For uncorrelated positions ($c = 0$), the two students follow the same learning trajectory, with the convolutional student learning exactly $P$ times faster. We also find that locality affects the sample complexity: a student that matches the kernel size of the teacher recovers it from $\mathcal{O}{D}(D)$ samples, whereas $\mathcal{O}{D}(D\log(D))$ samples are needed with a larger kernel. For $c > 0$, spatial correlations can reduce the advantage of weight sharing. The asymptotic error of the convolutional student grows with $c$, whereas that of the locally connected student is independent of $c$ and overall lower when evaluated at the same learning rate. When the learning rate is instead tuned to the training horizon, however, the locally connected student wins at early times and the convolutional student at late times, with a transition that we predict analytically.

link.title: Time-Uniform Dependent Central Limit Theory

entry.content:
We establish a near-optimal almost sure invariance principle for nonstationary time series under the functional dependence measure (FDM) framework. This result yields a universal time-uniform dependent central limit theorem, which serves as the basis for anytime-valid inference. In particular, we instantiate the theorem through asymptotic confidence sequences (AsympCSs), time-uniform counterparts of asymptotic confidence intervals obtained via central limit theorems, extending those originally proposed in Waudby-Smith et al. (2024) to time series with serial dependence. We further refine their definition because, as we show, it can admit AsympCSs that fail to achieve the desired asymptotic time-uniform coverage for a broad class of data-generating processes, including independent and identically distributed cases. We address this issue by adding a simple eventual-inclusion condition, which in turn permits more flexible variance estimation, particularly useful in time-series settings. For feasible implementation of AsympCSs, we establish strong consistency of HAC variance estimators under the FDM framework, accommodating a wider range of commonly used bandwidth choices than existing results under mixing conditions. As illustrations, we construct AsympCSs for algorithms with Markovian structure and time-series-based causal estimands.

entry.title: To Retain or to Adapt? Generalizing Continual Learning

link.title: To Retain or to Adapt? Generalizing Continual Learning

entry.content:
The Continual Learning (CL) literature has long been driven by the goal of mitigating catastrophic forgetting. This objective rests on an often unstated assumption: that a lifelong learner should approximate the Joint-Task Learning (JTL) solution and retain all previously acquired knowledge. We challenge this retention-centered premise, arguing that in non-stationary environments prioritizing retention can impede real-time adaptation. Shifting the focus to the Average Lifelong Error (ALE), we formalize CL as an online optimization problem governed by the interaction between environmental and learning dynamics. We introduce Transfer Efficiency as a quantitative measure of the tension between Instability, the bias inherited from conflicting past experience, and Transient Error, the optimization cost of learning new tasks from scratch. Under mild convergence conditions, holding across linear and neural network models, this decomposition yields a Critical Task Duration: a closed-form threshold beyond which historical knowledge transitions from a warm-start advantage to an optimization liability whenever retention induces a positive stationary bias. We validate these theoretical predictions on continual image classification and reinforcement learning benchmarks. Finally, by connecting continual learning to the online learning framework of predictable sequences, we show that JTL is only one instance of a broader family of objectives, and we propose a new general class of continual learning algorithms, which we call Predictive Continual Learning. Predictive CL algorithms optimize expected future performance under an explicit, dynamically updated model of future tasks. As a proof of concept, we analyze a Window algorithm that interpolates between JTL and Independent-Task Learning (ITL), outperforming both under controlled distributional drift.

link.title: Uniformly Improved Adaptive Filtering Procedures for Replicability Testing with FWER Control

entry.content:
Identifying signals that replicate across multiple studies is a fundamental challenge in modern data analysis. Partial conjunction (PC) testing addresses this problem by assessing whether a signal is present in at least a specified number of studies. The AdaFilter framework of Wang et al. (2022, Annals of Statistics 50, 1890-1909) improves the power of PC testing through adaptive filtering, but its family-wise error rate (FWER)-controlling procedures rely on conservative Bonferroni corrections at two stages: (i) the construction of PC $p$-values and filtering statistics, and (ii) the multiplicity adjustment used to control the FWER. We show that both stages can be improved using the \v{S}id'ak correction. Under the same independence assumptions as the original AdaFilter framework, our improvements preserve finite-sample FWER control and guarantee at least as many rejections as their Bonferroni counterparts for every realisation of the data. Simulations and a real data analysis demonstrate the practical benefits of these improvements.

entry.title: Using Temporal Replication and Partial Pooling to Improve Practical Identifiability in Presence-Only Poisson Point Process Models

link.title: Using Temporal Replication and Partial Pooling to Improve Practical Identifiability in Presence-Only Poisson Point Process Models

entry.content:
Species distribution models based on thinned point processes are now commonly used in ecology to analyze presence-only data collected through citizen science, including in spatio-temporal frameworks. A key challenge in these models is the separation of the ecological process from the observation process, which raises identifiability issues. Here, we investigate the theoretical and practical identifiability of a thinned Poisson point process model. We show that, with a log link for ecological intensity and a logit link for observation probability, the model can be structurally identifiable under simple conditions, provided that observation probability varies spatially. We then evaluate the benefits of using temporal replication within a spatio-temporal framework to improve estimation when ecological intensity and observation probability are weakly separated. We quantify these benefits through simulations. The results highlight persistent practical identifiability problems affecting the ecological and observation intercepts, especially when observation probabilities are low. However, in a spatio-temporal model with partial pooling, these parameters are estimated more accurately than in a single-year model, even when only a short time period is considered. Temporal replication also improves estimation of parameters shared across years. Finally, we illustrate the use of such a spatio-temporal model through a study of coypu (Myocastor coypus) distribution in Occitanie, France. Overall, our results show that temporal replication can partially alleviate practical identifiability problems in presence-only point process models when independent data sources are unavailable.

Overall, our results show that temporal replication can partially alleviate practical identifiability problems in presence-only point process models when independent data sources are unavailable.

entry.title: Vertex misalignment and changepoint localization in network time series

link.title: Vertex misalignment and changepoint localization in network time series

entry.content:
Inference for time series of networks often relies on accurate vertex correspondence between network realizations at different times. In practice, such vertex alignments can be misspecified or unknown. We study the impact of errorful vertex alignment on changepoint localization for dynamic networks through two illustrative models, with the key distinction being whether changepoint information is contained in marginal or joint distributions of the time-varying latent positions. We compare localization techniques ranging from the simple network statistic of average degree to the modern procedure of Euclidean mirrors. Our results demonstrate that understanding the interplay of marginal and joint information in the observed network time series is key to robust network inference.

entry.title: When Thoughts Become Memory: Unifying In-Context Learning and Fine-Tuning

link.title: When Thoughts Become Memory: Unifying In-Context Learning and Fine-Tuning

entry.content:
We are the first to give a certified rule for whether unseen data belong in a pretrained model’s context or its weights, built on an exact law for their information value. That value, the code length saved on held-out queries, equals in expectation the bits stored about the query, plus a prior repair, minus a decoding loss, for any model, architecture, dataset and task. The law’s ceilings certify the choice from one measurement, and an anytime-valid test makes it from held-out queries, with error controlled whenever it stops. Every certificate the ceilings issue on a trained transformer, TabPFN, an occupancy network and a stereo network is correct. The test picks TabPFN over XGBoost and a trained surrogate over an in-context learner on airfoil pressure, calls the better of GPT-2’s cache and fine-tune in 61,948 of 64,000 query streams over 32 comparisons, and errs in at most 3.3% of null streams. The law also diagnoses when learning in context helps and when it does not. Deleting part of a context is held-out validation of that part in any model, and adding parts one at a time traces the learning curve in context: one patch that sees a shape feature cuts an occupancy network’s code length there a hundredfold, while eight that miss it nearly double it, and one camera that sees the surface beats four in a stereo network. Ranked by this label-free valuation, a kriging learner’s three best support cars beat four drawn at random, and on a yes-or-no claim the valuation recovers a published evidence adjudicator, with AUROC 0.91.

entry.title: When Windowed Anderson Acceleration Converges Faster

link.title: When Windowed Anderson Acceleration Converges Faster

entry.content:
Windowed Anderson acceleration AA($m$) combines at most $m+1$ recent iterates by least squares. For a real affine contraction $x\mapsto Wx+b$ with $q=|W| \in(0,1)$, we determine exactly when AA($m$) converges from every starting point with an asymptotic factor below $q$. We give a polynomial criterion for this improvement and an equivalent spectral condition: there is no probability distribution on the phases of the eigenvalues of modulus $q$ whose first $m$ cosine moments are $q,q^2,\ldots,q^m$. If such a distribution exists, we construct a starting point from which AA($m$) reproduces fixed-point iteration at every step. Otherwise, over a fixed number of consecutive steps, every run contracts the residual norm by a common factor strictly smaller than the corresponding power of $q$. The polynomial criterion also gives explicit convergence-rate bounds with constants independent of the dimension. When $q$ equals the spectral radius, this characterizes improvement over the asymptotic convergence factor of fixed-point iteration. For general affine contractions, the asymptotic factor never exceeds the numerical radius of $W$, and a related moment condition gives a uniform upper bound strictly below that radius.
